**Mastercard adds trust and intelligence layer to agentic payments programme**

*The expansion of Agent Pay moves beyond transaction execution to address the verification and context gaps that have slowed enterprise adoption of AI-initiated payments.*

Mastercard has expanded Agent Pay, its agentic payments programme, with new trust and intelligence services designed to give merchants and financial institutions greater context about AI-initiated transactions. The services aim to verify the identity and authorisation of AI agents acting on behalf of consumers or businesses before a payment is processed.

Agentic commerce has moved rapidly from concept to live pilots over the past six months, with Visa, Mastercard, Blik and several European banks all completing agentic transactions. The bottleneck is no longer whether agents can initiate payments but whether the surrounding infrastructure can authenticate them reliably. Mastercard's move addresses this directly, building a verification layer on top of the payment rail rather than treating agent identity as someone else's problem.

The announcement follows EMVCo's draft framework for card-based agentic payments published in September and the formation of a cross-industry agentic payments alliance. Trust infrastructure is emerging as the competitive battleground: whoever defines how agents are credentialled and monitored will shape the economics of the channel.

*Sources: [Mastercard rolls out trust and intelligence services for agentic commerce](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/111213/mastercard-rolls-out-trust-and-intelligence-services-for-agentic-commerce?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*

**EU and UK banks face one-year countdown to T+1 settlement**

*Treasury operations and liquidity management across European banks and payment processors with capital markets exposure must be overhauled before the October 2027 deadline for next-day securities settlement.*

The transition to T+1 settlement, which compresses the post-trade window from two business days to one, gives banks in the EU and the UK one year to demonstrate operational readiness. The deadline, set for October 2027, follows the US move to T+1 in May 2024 and brings European markets into alignment.

The operational burden falls disproportionately on firms that operate across time zones or rely on manual processes for funding, foreign exchange and reconciliation. For payments firms with treasury or liquidity functions tied to securities settlement, the compressed cycle will tighten intraday liquidity requirements and demand more automation in cash positioning. Banks already under pressure from the SEPA instant payments regulation's liquidity demands face a second, parallel squeeze.

Unlike the US transition, which applied to a single market, the European move must be coordinated across multiple central securities depositories and national regulators simultaneously. The complexity is structural, not just technical.

*Sources: [EU and UK banks face 1 year deadline for T+1](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48564/eu-and-uk-banks-face-1-year-deadline-for-t1?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*
